planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring to early summer; Creeping Raspberry roots readily wherever its trailing stems touch soil, so a single plant fills in as a dense mat within a season or two in partial shade.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun, spacing plants to knit together into a solid groundcover; established plantings tolerate light foot traffic and need only occasional shearing to keep them tidy. Creeping Raspberry is a low, evergreen-to-semi-evergreen trailing bramble native to Taiwan, grown chiefly as an ornamental groundcover for its glossy, crinkled, bronze-tinged leaves, small white flowers, and small orange-red, raspberry-like fruits produced in late summer that are edible, if mild and seedy, and readily eaten by birds. Its dense, mounding, self-rooting habit makes it useful for covering slopes, edging shaded beds, or spilling over walls in areas too shady for turfgrass, and unlike upright brambles it stays low and thornless-feeling underfoot. Cut back hard in late winter every few years to renew growth and prevent the center of the planting from thinning out.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Rubus pentalobus Plant Profile
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Groundcovers for Shade

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January-February in zone 9); Excel is a Type I pollinator (sheds pollen before its own pistillate flowers are receptive) and needs a Type II cultivar such as Elliott or Desirable nearby for cross-pollination and full nut set.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Excel is a modern Louisiana-bred pecan cultivar selected for strong resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum), the humid-climate fungal disease that plagues many older commercial cultivars along the Gulf Coast, reducing or eliminating the need for fungicide sprays in home plantings. It produces large, well-filled nuts with good kernel quality and ripens relatively early, helping it escape late-season disease and weather pressure. Because of its disease tolerance, Excel is increasingly recommended for Gulf South home orchards where spray programs are impractical. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and watch for zinc deficiency on alkaline soils, correcting with a foliar zinc spray in spring.
sources: LSU AgCenter — Pecan Variety Recommendations for Louisiana

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January-February in zone 9); Forkert is a Type II pollinator and needs a Type I cultivar such as Excel or Cape Fear nearby for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Forkert is a classic Mississippi pecan cultivar valued for its thin, papery shell that cracks out easily in large, whole kernel halves, along with rich flavor and good kernel percentage. It bears precociously and produces consistent crops in the Gulf South, though like many older cultivars it benefits from a fungicide program in wet years to manage pecan scab. Forkert is commonly recommended alongside scab-resistant cultivars in home orchard plantings to diversify harvest timing and pollination. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and correct zinc deficiency with a foliar zinc spray each spring on alkaline soils.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — Pecan Cultivars for Mississippi

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January-February in zone 9); Curtis is a Type II pollinator and needs a Type I cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination and full nut set.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Curtis is an old, Florida Panhandle-origin pecan cultivar valued for its outstanding resistance to pecan scab and other humid-climate fungal diseases, making it one of the most reliable low-spray options for Deep South home orchards. The nuts are smaller than many modern commercial cultivars but well filled, with good flavor, and the tree bears consistently and precociously once established. Because of its disease tolerance and long track record along the Gulf Coast, Curtis is frequently recommended as a dependable, low-maintenance pollinator and production tree for home growers who do not want to run a fungicide spray program. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and correct zinc deficiency with a foliar zinc spray each spring.
